meeting_header:
Date: 2028-09-14
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Evan Carter (Redwood AE), Lina Park (Redwood SE), Ravi Singh (Redwood Solutions), Maya Chen (Verdant SRE), Rohan Patel (Verdant Head of MLOps), Samir Khatri (Verdant Security), Tessa Nguyen (Verdant Product)
summary: Initial reliability & incident-tolerance discovery focused on fallback policies, multi-region routing, and SLA alignment. Customer evaluating Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private for production LLM inference. Key concerns: data residency, KMS integration, predictable tail latency under regional failures, and runbook automation. Agreed next steps: security pack, fallback policy template, pilot kickoff week of Sep 25.
topics: Fallback policy options (circuit breakers, canary rollouts, region steering)
Multi-region routing and failover latency impact
Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs for security and predictability
transcript:
[00:00] Evan (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros?
[00:12] Maya (Verdant): Hi I'm Maya, SRE on Verdant infra. We're looking at Redwood for inference for a customer-critical pipeline.
[00:20] Rohan (Verdant): Rohan, head of MLOps. primary concerns are tail latency and predictable unit costs when we hit spikes.
[00:28] Evan: Great. Lina are you on the line to cover fallback options?
[00:32] Lina (Redwood SE): Yep I'm here. I'll walk through routing and degraded modes. Quick note — sorry if the demo deck link in the invite had a typo, i fixed it and put the fallback diagram in the chat.
[01:00] Tessa (Verdant): Quick question up front, we're evaluating Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private — can Redwood guarantee SLOs across a failover?
[01:12] Evan: short answer — we have SLA tiers for Dedicated and committed capacity; hosted has best-effort SLAs but we surface per-route latency percentiles. For guaranteed SLOs we typically recommend Dedicated or Private with reserved pools.
[01:30] Samir (Security): And on data residency and KMS — we need customer-managed keys and an audit trail for all inference requests.
[01:40] Lina: For Private we support KMS/HSM integrations and detailed audit logs, for Dedicated we can do KMS-integration as part of the contract, hosted supports envelope encryption but not CMK in all regions today — we'll send the exact matrix.
[02:05] Maya: What's the expected behavior when a region goes down? Do we have automatic region-steering or do we need a DNS-level switch?
[02:15] Lina: Redwood supports policy-based routing. Options: active-active with region steering, hot standby in secondary region, and traffic-split with automatics fallback. We can do client-side DNS TTL low, or use our routing plane to steer. There's also an auto-fallback policy that avoids cold starts by keeping warm caches in a secondary.
[03:05] Ravi (Redwood): Important nuance — for large KV cache warmup you can see a brief tail-latency spike if you cold-start a secondary model variant; our prefix caching and pre-warm hooks aim to reduce that.
[03:25] Rohan: That warms my concern — what's the typical spike magnitude? 99.9 percentile goes from 120ms to 900ms?
[03:33] Lina: It depends. For text-gen real workloads we've seen 99.9 go up 2-6x on cold fallback without cached KVs. With proactive cache-warm (we can prefetch top-k prompts) and smaller sequence lengths you can keep it within 1.5-2x. We'll share concrete bench numbers.
[04:10] Maya: If we do Dedicated, can we pin model versions and have canary rollouts between two pools so fallback is seamless?
[04:20] Evan: Yes — Dedicated supports model pinning and rollout policies. Canary -> A/B -> full. You can also configure automatic fallback to previous stable model if quality drifts.
[04:38] Samir: Audit logs — are those at token level or request metadata? We need traceability for every request id.
[04:48] Lina: We emit request-level logs with model, route, latency, user id hash, and optional token-level counts. For Private we can ship full audit logs into your SIEM.
[05:12] Tessa: Cost tradeoffs — if we keep warm replicas in multiple regions what's the cost delta?
[05:20] Ravi: Warm replicas cost is mainly reserved GPU hours plus storage for KV caches. Typically warm hot-standby in a second region adds ~30-60% to baseline depending on utilization. The Optimize playbook recommends using regional listen thresholds to only keep minimal warm capacity until health events trigger scale up.
[05:55] Rohan: On routing: how fast can we detect a regional outage and fail traffic — seconds, or minutes?
[06:03] Lina: Detection is multi-layered. We have health checks at infra and application level plus external probes. Typical detection to failover is 15-45s for automated policies; full shift depends on TCP session draining and client retry behavior.
[06:30] Maya: Our product requires 99.95 uptime per month at 95% of our traffic. We need to map Redwood SLAs to contract clauses.
[06:42] Evan: We'll map Redwood's SLA tiers to your SLOs. If Dedicated with X reserved capacity we can commit to p99/p99.9 latency targets and uptime SLAs. For hosted we'll provide best-effort and suggested fallbacks.
[07:05] Samir: Another security point — do you keep KV cache in plaintext on GPU memory or encrypted? Are there consent logs for data exfil?
[07:20] Lina: KV cache in memory isn't persisted in plaintext; for Private deployments you control the host and KMS. We'll include a security note on memory handling and recommendations for bring-your-own-key.
[07:42] Tessa: Can you talk about degraded modes — what behavior should our app expect if you only have capacity for embeddings but not full generation?
[07:55] Ravi: We support graceful degradation: you can configure route-specific fallbacks (e.g., return cached response, degrade to shorter candidate models, or return soft-failure with a retry token). There's an SDK hook to detect degraded-mode and show a user-facing message.
[08:25] Rohan: For our regulatory customers we might need Private inside our VPC. How different is the operational experience?
[08:34] Lina: Private is the same API surface, but you run control plane in your VPC. You'll manage networking and have full access to logs. We provide operators runbooks and we can run an on-prem packaging if needed. The big difference is control over KMS and audit surface.
[09:02] Maya: Let's circle back to failover cost — if we route 30% to a cheaper quantized model during outages, how much latency penalty and quality drop do we expect?
[09:14] Lina: Quantized models typically add small latency improvements but some quality delta for sensitive tasks. For safety-critical prompts we recommend hybrid routing: attempts to primary full-precision, fallback to quantized only for non-critical queries. We'll provide eval diffs for your prompt set.
[09:45] Tessa: Are there built-in rollbacks if a canary causes quality regression?
[09:52] Evan: Yes — automated rollback policies based on eval sets and A/B metric thresholds. You can configure automatic rollback at X% drop in eval quality or on error-rate spikes.
[10:10] Maya: Ok can we define acceptance criteria for fallback? For example: under simulated regional failure, 95% of requests must meet 150ms p99 within 5 minutes of failover.
[10:25] Lina: That's reasonable. We'll help you design a chaos test. We can run a pilot with synthetic traffic to validate 99/99.9 behavior and measure degradation curves.
[11:05] Rohan: On telemetry — will Redwood emit traces we can ingest? e.g. span ids and request ids for cross-service tracing?
[11:12] Ravi: Yes we emit request ids and support OpenTelemetry spans; for Private you can export directly to your tracing backend. For hosted we support pushing traces to your collector via secure endpoint.
[11:45] Samir: How's rate limiting handled in failover? If primary is saturated and we shift traffic to secondary, do tokens/quotas transfer or do we risk immediate throttling?
[11:58] Lina: Rate limits are per-account and can be configured per-route. In Dedicated there is capacity isolation so you won't get throttled on failover if you've reserved burst capacity. In hosted, sudden shifts can trigger quota throttles — our recommendation is to have burst reserve or a gradual ramp policy.
[12:25] Maya: For the pilot, we want to scope tests: 1) regional outage simulation, 2) canary rollback test, 3) degraded-model routing test. Can Redwood run the infra side and Verdant run the client-side checks?
[12:40] Evan: Absolutely. We'll propose a pilot plan in the follow-up. Lina will own the fallback templates.
[13:00] --[light cross talk]--
[20:15] (transcription gap)
[21:10] Rohan: Let's talk timelines. We're aiming to pick a vendor and start pilot by end of September; full prod in Q4. Any blockers you foresee?
[21:25] Evan: Security review is biggest. If Private is required that adds procurement lead time for networking and on-prem packaging. We'll fast-track the SOC2 pack.
[22:05] Samir: We need SAML SSO and org-level RBAC and proof of employee access controls.
[22:15] Lina: All supported; we'll include SSO docs and RBAC capabilities in the pack.
[25:00] Maya: A small nit — how is model fallback logged for auditing? We need to know if a response came from fallback route vs primary.
[25:10] Ravi: Every response has metadata: route id, model id, region, and fallback flag. That gets into the audit log stream.
[30:45] Tessa: On legal — can you support a clause about mandatory notification windows for incidents?
[30:55] Evan: Yes, standard incident notification windows are 1 hour for Sev1 in Dedicated/Enterprise; we can align contract language during procurement.
[33:10] Maya: Are there examples of customers running active-active across 3 regions with Redwood?
[33:20] Lina: Yes, a couple of media and fintech customers run 3-region active-active with our routing plane; we've published a technical note — we'll include case references.
[35:00] Rohan: For the pilot metrics, we'll capture 50k requests/min sustained spike test and measure p95/p99/p99.9 pre/post failover.
[35:12] Evan: Good. Also we'll instrument synthetic prompts to validate semantic quality during fallback.
[36:50] (minor crosstalk)
[40:05] Lina: Summarizing fallback policy variants: 1) Active-active region steering with load-weighted routing and cache warmers, 2) Hot standby with pre-warmed KV cache, 3) Traffic-split with progressive ramp and circuit-breaker thresholds, 4) Degraded-model fallback to quantized variants.
[40:40] Maya: Which do you recommend for our use case?
[40:44] Lina: Given your regulatory needs and desire for stable p99, Dedicated with hot-standby in a secondary region plus progressive traffic-split is our recommendation. If Private is needed for data residency, same topology applies but with more control and slightly longer lead time.
[41:05] Samir: We'll need a clear runbook for escalation — who's oncall at Redwood during pilot?
[41:13] Evan: We'll assign an SE and an SRE liaison for the pilot; contact list will be included.
[41:40] Tessa: Any limitation on model size or kv cache when using private?
[41:48] Lina: Private supports same model architectures; limits are driven by node sizing. We can size GPUs to match your KV footprint.
[42:20] (brief pause)
[45:00] Evan: Quick recap and next steps: action items — security pack, fallback template, cost/latency spreadsheet, pilot kickoff. We'll aim to get the docs out this week.
[45:22] Maya: Sounds good. Also we'll share our perf histo and target SLAs by Monday.
[45:30] Rohan: One more technical — can Redwood do traffic shadowing to the secondary region without affecting production?
[45:38] Ravi: Yes we support shadowing and traffic mirroring for model evaluation. You can do shadow test with real traffic and analyze quality metrics.
[46:10] Samir: For the SOC2 pack, please include details on employee access revocation and key rotation frequency.
[46:20] Evan: noted.
[51:00] Tessa: Ok that's all from us, thanks everyone.
[51:08] Evan: Thanks all — we'll follow up with the packet and propose pilot timeslots.
[51:15] Lina: Bye.
[51:20] (recording ends)
